lec05kp19-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp19-u01-p1-title.text: The SVM rule touches the data only through inner products xᵢᵀx, and after a map only yᵢᵀy

lec05kp19-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp19-u01-p1-bridge.text: The PNN of KP18 keeps every training point. Is there a way to keep only a few points and still classify nonlinearly?

lec05kp19-u01-p1-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp19-inner
lec05kp19-u01-p1-fig1.text: Flow of the SVM rule: x, the inner product xᵢᵀx and sign(g); the data enter only through inner products, and the worry is the cost when the map to k dimensions has k much larger than l.

image.alt: Flow of the SVM rule: x, the inner product xᵢᵀx and sign(g); the data enter only through inner products, and the worry is the cost when the map to k dimensions has k much larger than l.

lec05kp19-u01-p1-term:支撐向量.name: term:Support vector
lec05kp19-u01-p1-term:支撐向量.text: **Support vectors**: the training points whose weight $\lambda_i>0$ after training; the rule depends on them alone, and there are usually far fewer than all the training points.

lec05kp19-u01-p1-c1.name: u01-p1-c1
lec05kp19-u01-p1-c1.text: **The rule**: $g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}\lambda_iy_i\,x_i^Tx+w_0$ with $x$ of dimension $l$ and $N_s$ support vectors; the data enter only through the inner product $x_i^Tx$.

lec05kp19-u01-p1-c2.name: u01-p1-c2
lec05kp19-u01-p1-c2.text: **The idea and the naive worry**: design in a $k$-dimensional space by using $\phi(x_i)^T\phi(x)$; but $k\gg l$, so surely the cost explodes?

lec05kp19-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp19-u01-p2-title.text: Map to [x₁², √2·x₁x₂, x₂²]: the 3-D inner product equals the square of the 2-D one

lec05kp19-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp19-u01-p2-bridge.text: The naive worry was that the cost explodes when $k\gg l$. Take one concrete map: how is the mapped inner product $\phi(x_i)^T\phi(x_j)$ computed?

lec05kp19-u01-p2-term:核函數.name: term:Kernel function
lec05kp19-u01-p2-term:核函數.text: **Kernel function** $K(x,z)$: a function that gives the mapped inner product $\phi(x)^T\phi(z)$ directly, without computing the map first.

lec05kp19-u01-p2-c2.name: u01-p2-c2
lec05kp19-u01-p2-c2.text: **Check**: $x_i=(1,2)$, $x_j=(2,1)$: $\phi(x_i)=(1,2.828,4)$, $\phi(x_j)=(4,2.828,1)$, inner product $4+8+4=16$; the original space gives $4^2=16$, the same; the high-dimensional vectors never have to be built.

lec05kp19-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp19-u01-p3-title.text: Two rings cannot be split in 2-D, but after the map the line y₁+y₃ = ‖x‖² splits them

lec05kp19-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp19-u01-p3-bridge.text: The high-dimensional inner product is just the square of the original-space inner product. Can this map really make inseparable concentric rings separable?

lec05kp19-u01-p3-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp19-lift
lec05kp19-u01-p3-fig1.text: Left: concentric rings that no line separates in 2-D; right: in the coordinates y₁ and y₃ after the map, the line y₁+y₃=2.5 cuts 97.5% right.

image.alt: Left: concentric rings that no line separates in 2-D; right: in the coordinates y₁ and y₃ after the map, the line y₁+y₃=2.5 cuts 97.5% right.

lec05kp19-u01-p3-c1.name: u01-p3-c1
lec05kp19-u01-p3-c1.text: **Data** (designed here): two concentric rings of radius about 1 and 2 (sd 0.25), 60 training and a separate 100 new points per class.

lec05kp19-u01-p3-c2.name: u01-p3-c2
lec05kp19-u01-p3-c2.text: **After the map**: $y_1+y_3=x_1^2+x_2^2=\|x\|^2$, so the map turns the radius into a coordinate; the line $y_1+y_3=2.5$ cuts between the rings.

lec05kp19-u01-p3-c3.name: u01-p3-c3
lec05kp19-u01-p3-c3.text: **Result**: one cut gets 97.5% of 200 new points (100 per class) right, a few overlapping at the edges; a plane in 3-D is a circle in the original space.

lec05kp19-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp19-u01-p4-title.text: Mercer's theorem: a legal K has a space behind it, and K is its inner product

lec05kp19-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp19-u01-p4-bridge.text: The concentric rings were cut by a linear classifier after the map. For any other function $K$, how do we know a mapped space stands behind it too?

lec05kp19-u01-p4-term:Mercer 條件.name: term:Mercer condition
lec05kp19-u01-p4-term:Mercer 條件.text: **Mercer condition**: $K$ is symmetric and continuous and $\iint K(x,z)g(x)g(z)\,dx\,dz\ge0$ for every square-integrable $g$.

lec05kp19-u01-p4-c1.name: u01-p4-c1
lec05kp19-u01-p4-c1.text: **Theorem**: a $K$ meeting the condition has a space $H$ and a map $\phi$ with $K(x,z)=\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle$, and conversely; it does not say what $\phi$ or $H$ look like (the Gaussian $H$ is infinite-dimensional).

lec05kp19-u01-p4-c3.name: u01-p4-c3
lec05kp19-u01-p4-c3.text: **A finite check** (added): the Gram matrix $[K(x_i,x_j)]$ must be positive semidefinite; 30 random points: smallest eigenvalue $8.8\times10^{-8}$ (Gaussian), $-8\times10^{-15}$ (quadratic, rounding).

lec05kp19-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp19-u01-p5-title.text: Replace xᵢᵀxⱼ by K(xᵢ, xⱼ) in the SVM and the original space gets a nonlinear classifier

lec05kp19-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp19-u01-p5-bridge.text: Mercer's theorem gives any $K$ meeting the condition a space behind it. How must the SVM change to actually use it?

lec05kp19-u01-p5-c1.name: u01-p5-c1
lec05kp19-u01-p5-c1.text: **Common kernels**: polynomial $(x^Tz+1)^q$; Gaussian $\exp(-\gamma\|x-z\|^2)$; hyperbolic tangent $\tanh(\beta x^Tz+\gamma)$ (see extension).

lec05kp19-u01-p5-c2.name: u01-p5-c2
lec05kp19-u01-p5-c2.text: **The dual problem**: $\max_\lambda\ \sum_i\lambda_i-\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\lambda_i\lambda_jy_iy_jK(x_i,x_j)$ with $0\le\lambda_i\le C$ and $\sum_i\lambda_iy_i=0$; $C$ caps the penalty for violations.

lec05kp19-u01-p5-c3.name: u01-p5-c3
lec05kp19-u01-p5-c3.text: **The rule**: $g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}\lambda_iy_iK(x_i,x)+w_0$, and $g>0$ goes to $\omega_1$. Check (added): with the solved $\lambda$ this formula differs from the library's decision value by at most $10^{-14}$.

lec05kp19-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp19-u01-p6-title.text: On the rings: the linear kernel gets only 56.2%, the quadratic 97.6% and the Gaussian 96.8%

lec05kp19-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp19-u01-p6-bridge.text: With the common kernels in the dual problem, how much do the linear, quadratic and Gaussian kernels get right on the concentric rings?

lec05kp19-u01-p6-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp19-regions
lec05kp19-u01-p6-fig1.text: Decision regions and support vectors (circles) of three kernels on the rings: linear 56.2% with 118, quadratic 97.6% with 10, Gaussian 96.8% with 19.

image.alt: Decision regions and support vectors (circles) of three kernels on the rings: linear 56.2% with 118, quadratic 97.6% with 10, Gaussian 96.8% with 19.

lec05kp19-u01-p6-c1.name: u01-p6-c1
lec05kp19-u01-p6-c1.text: **Setup** (designed here): concentric rings, 60 training and 500 new points per class; $C=10$, Gaussian $\gamma=0.5$, quadratic $(x^Tz+1)^2$.

lec05kp19-u01-p6-c2.name: u01-p6-c2
lec05kp19-u01-p6-c2.text: **Results** (new points): linear 56.2% with 118 support vectors; quadratic 97.6% with 10; Gaussian 96.8% with 19.

lec05kp19-u01-p6-c3.name: u01-p6-c3
lec05kp19-u01-p6-c3.text: **Meaning**: same data and algorithm, only the kernel changes, from near guessing to about 97%; the Gaussian kernel keeps 19 support vectors where a PNN keeps all 120 training points (compare KP21).

lec05kp19-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp19-u01-p7-title.text: C and γ steer generalization: at γ = 50 training reaches 99.2%, new points 74.7%

lec05kp19-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp19-u01-p7-bridge.text: The Gaussian kernel keeps 19 support vectors, but γ and C must be fixed first. What if they go up or down?

lec05kp19-u01-p7-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp19-hyper
lec05kp19-u01-p7-fig1.text: On more overlapping rings, training and new-point accuracy against the Gaussian γ: 87.0% on new points at γ=0.1 is best, while γ=50 gives 99.2% on training and 74.7% on new points.

image.alt: On more overlapping rings, training and new-point accuracy against the Gaussian γ: 87.0% on new points at γ=0.1 is best, while γ=50 gives 99.2% on training and 74.7% on new points.

lec05kp19-u01-p7-term:超參數.name: term:Hyperparameter
lec05kp19-u01-p7-term:超參數.text: **Hyperparameter**: set before training, not solved from the data: here $\gamma$ and $C$.

lec05kp19-u01-p7-c1.name: u01-p7-c1
lec05kp19-u01-p7-c1.text: **Method** (designed here): overlapping rings (sd 0.45); per class 60 training, 500 validation, 500 test points; $C=10$.

lec05kp19-u01-p7-c3.name: u01-p7-c3
lec05kp19-u01-p7-c3.text: **Choosing**: read the validation column, pick $\gamma=0.5$, $C=10$: test 86.1%; peeking at the test column for $\gamma=0.1$ gives 87.0%, optimistic.

lec05kp19-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp19-u01-p8-title.text: The cost ignores the kernel-space dimension: 2.5×10¹² features, about 784 multiplications

lec05kp19-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp19-u01-p8-bridge.text: The hyperparameter γ and the penalty cap C must be set before training. Looking back: the kernel space is huge, so why is it cheap?

lec05kp19-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp19-u01-p8-c1.text: **Explicit features**: a polynomial kernel of dimension $l$ and degree $q$ has $\binom{l+q}{q}$ features: $(2,2)$: 6; $(10,3)$: 286; $(100,5)$: 96,560,646; $(784,5)$: 2,515,874,132,157.

lec05kp19-u01-p8-c2.name: u01-p8-c2
lec05kp19-u01-p8-c2.text: **One kernel value**: an inner product and a power, about $l$ multiplications whatever the kernel-space dimension; the infinite-dimensional Gaussian space still costs one distance.

lec05kp19-u01-p8-c3.name: u01-p8-c3
lec05kp19-u01-p8-c3.text: **Limit**: training still needs an $N\times N$ Gram matrix. **To remember**: an algorithm that uses only inner products can be lifted to a higher dimension; the price is not knowing the space.

lec05kp19-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp19-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: the tanh kernel can be illegal, with a negative eigenvalue in 200 of 200 draws

lec05kp19-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp19-u01-p9-bridge.text: Any algorithm using only inner products can be lifted to a higher dimension, but nobody knows how to pick the best kernel. Is the common hyperbolic-tangent kernel always legal?

lec05kp19-u01-p9-c1.name: u01-p9-c1
lec05kp19-u01-p9-c1.text: **Example** (designed here): $K=\tanh(2x^Tz+1)$ on the three points $(-1,0)$, $(1.6,0.9)$, $(0.1,-0.8)$ gives a Gram matrix with eigenvalues $-0.132$, $0.875$ and $2.232$.

lec05kp19-u01-p9-c2.name: u01-p9-c2
lec05kp19-u01-p9-c2.text: **Result**: a negative eigenvalue violates the Mercer condition; with 10 random points drawn 200 times the tanh kernel has one in all 200, the Gaussian kernel in 0.

lec05kp19-u01-p9-c3.name: u01-p9-c3
lec05kp19-u01-p9-c3.text: **Meaning**: $\tanh$ with $(\beta=2,\gamma=1)$ is not a legal kernel and the dual need not be convex (inferred, not measured); check first or use the Gaussian.

lec05kp19-u01-p10-title.name: u01-p10-title
lec05kp19-u01-p10-title.text: Extension: practice, the value of the quadratic kernel and the 6-feature map

lec05kp19-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp19-u01-p10-bridge.text: The hyperbolic-tangent kernel can be illegal. Back to the legal quadratic kernel $K=(x^Tz+1)^2$: how is the kernel value of two vectors computed?

lec05kp19-u01-p10-q3.name: u01-p10-q3
lec05kp19-u01-p10-q3.text: **Question 2**: compute the 6 features $\phi(x)$ and $\phi(z)$, take their inner product and check it against Question 1.

lec05kp19-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp19-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: worked solution of questions 1 and 2, both ways give 36

lec05kp19-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp19-u01-p11-bridge.text: The practice asked for the value of the quadratic kernel and the 6-feature map. Worked out in full, what do the two ways give?

lec05kp19-u01-p11-a3.name: u01-p11-a3
lec05kp19-u01-p11-a3.text: **Check**: the same 36; the kernel works in 2-D while the map first builds 6 features, and the gap widens with dimension (see the feature-count table).

steps.label: Kernel SVM
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 8 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Made under CLARITY.md C12 to C18. The fact that the SVM uses only inner products, the quadratic-map identity, Mercer's theorem and what it does not tell us, the kernelized dual and decision rule, the complexity independent of the kernel-space dimension and the 'to remember' line follow the source; every number (the identity check 16, the concentric-ring accuracies of 56.2% for the linear kernel, 97.6% for the quadratic and 96.8% for the Gaussian, the support-vector counts, the sweeps of gamma and C, the feature-count table, the negative eigenvalues of the hyperbolic-tangent kernel, the practice answer 36) was recomputed by a program and these experiments were designed for this lecture (added); the pages state honestly that the rings overlap, that new points drop to 74.7% when gamma is too large, and that training still grows with the number of training points. Speaker notes are published with the file and contain no student numbers, grades or exam items.

steps.label: Inner products only
steps.speakerNotes: The PNN of KP18 keeps every training point. This page asks whether there is a way to keep only a few points and still classify nonlinearly. First support vectors: the training points whose weight lambda is above zero after training, on which the rule alone depends, usually far fewer than all the training points. The rule is the sum over the support vectors of lambda times y times an inner product, plus w0; the data enter only through inner products. The idea: to design in a k-dimensional mapped space, replace the vectors by their images y and the inner product by y_i transpose y. The naive worry: k much larger than l, so surely the complexity explodes? The figure shows the flow of this rule. The next page looks at a concrete map and the answer is a pleasant surprise.

steps.label: A quadratic map
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page worried that the complexity would explode. This page takes one concrete map and asks how the mapped inner product is computed. First the kernel function K: a function that gives the mapped inner product directly, without computing the map first. The identity: for y equal to x1 squared, root 2 times x1 x2, and x2 squared, y_i transpose y_j equals the square of x_i transpose x_j. Check: x_i is (1, 2) and x_j is (2, 1); y_i is (1, 2.828, 4) and y_j is (4, 2.828, 1), with inner product 4 plus 8 plus 4, which is 16; in the original space 1 times 2 plus 2 times 1 is 4, and its square is also 16, the same. The meaning is that the high-dimensional inner product comes from the original-space inner product, so the high-dimensional vectors never have to be built. The next page asks whether this map really makes inseparable data separable.

steps.label: Lifting the rings
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the high-dimensional inner product is just the square of the original-space inner product. This page asks whether this map really makes inseparable concentric rings separable. The data were designed here: two concentric rings of radius about 1 and 2 with standard deviation 0.25, 60 training and 500 new points per class. After the map y1 plus y3 equals x1 squared plus x2 squared, the squared radius, so the map turns the radius into a coordinate; the line y1 plus y3 equal to 2.5 cuts between the rings. The result: one cut gets 97.5% of 200 new points right, 100 per class, a few overlapping at the edges. It is a linear classifier in 3-D and a circle in the original space. The figure leaves out the middle coordinate. The next page asks how to know that any other function K has such a space behind it.

steps.label: Mercer's theorem
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the concentric rings were cut by a linear classifier after the map. This page asks how we know that any other function K has a mapped space behind it. First the Mercer condition: K is symmetric and continuous and the double integral of K times g times g is at least zero for every square-integrable g. The theorem: a K meeting the condition has a space H and a map phi such that K is the inner product of phi, and conversely. What it does not say: nothing about what phi looks like or the dimension of H; the space of the Gaussian kernel is infinite-dimensional. A finite check, added here: the Gram matrix must be positive semidefinite. For 30 random points the smallest eigenvalue is 8.8 times 10 to the minus 8 for the Gaussian kernel and minus 8 times 10 to the minus 15 for the quadratic one, which is rounding and taken as zero. The next page asks how to change the SVM to use it.

steps.label: The kernelized SVM
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said Mercer's theorem gives a legal K a space behind it. This page asks how the SVM must change to actually use it. Three common kernels: polynomial, Gaussian and hyperbolic tangent. The dual problem: replace the inner product by K, with the constraints unchanged, lambda between 0 and C and the sum of lambda times y equal to zero; C caps the penalty for violations. The rule: the sum over the support vectors of lambda times y times K, plus w0, and a positive value goes to the first class. I checked that with the solved lambda this formula differs from the library's decision value by at most 10 to the minus 14. Because the kernel is nonlinear, this is a nonlinear classifier in the original space. The next page asks how the three kernels do on the concentric rings.

steps.label: The rings experiment
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page put the kernelized rule in place. This page asks how much the linear, quadratic and Gaussian kernels get right on the concentric rings. The setup was designed here: concentric rings, 60 training and 500 new points per class; C equal to 10, Gaussian gamma equal to 0.5 and the quadratic kernel x transpose z plus 1, squared. The results on new points: the linear kernel 56.2% with 118 support vectors, the quadratic 97.6% with 10 and the Gaussian 96.8% with 19. The meaning is that data and algorithm stayed the same and only the kernel changed, from near guessing to about 97%; the Gaussian kernel keeps 19 support vectors where a PNN keeps all 120 training points, compared again in KP21. The circled points in the figure are the support vectors. The next page asks how to choose the Gaussian gamma and C.

steps.label: Hyperparameters
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the Gaussian kernel keeps only 19 support vectors. This page asks what happens when its gamma and C, which must be fixed beforehand, go up or down. First hyperparameters: parameters set before training rather than solved from the data, here the Gaussian gamma and the penalty cap C. The data were split in three: 60 training points per class, 500 per class for validation and 500 per class for test, and the hyperparameters were chosen on the validation data. Results, training correct out of 120, validation and test correct out of 1000: gamma 0.1 gives 106, 863 and 870; gamma 0.5 gives 106, 866 and 861, the highest on validation; gamma 50 gives 119, 753 and 747. For C with gamma 0.5, C of 10 is highest on validation. Taking the validation choice, gamma 0.5 and C 10, to the test gives 861 out of 1000, 86.1%; peeking at the test column and picking gamma 0.1 would give 87.0%, a picked number that is optimistic. A tighter fit to training does not always help new points. The next page asks why it is cheap when the kernel space is so large.

steps.label: Dimension-free
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the hyperparameters gamma and C must be fixed beforehand. This page asks, looking back, why it is still cheap when the kernel space is so large. Explicit feature counts: a polynomial kernel of dimension l and degree q corresponds to l plus q choose q features: l equal to 2 and q equal to 2 gives 6; l equal to 10 and q equal to 3 gives 286; l equal to 100 and q equal to 5 gives 96,560,646; l equal to 784 and q equal to 5 gives 2,515,874,132,157. One kernel value: an inner product and a power, about l multiplications, independent of the kernel-space dimension; the Gaussian space is infinite-dimensional yet costs one distance. The limits: training still needs an N by N Gram matrix and grows with the number of points, and nobody knows how to pick the best kernel. To remember: the kernel trick says any algorithm that uses only inner products can be lifted to a higher dimension; the price is not knowing which space you are in. The next extension page looks at an illegal kernel.

steps.label: Extension: illegal kernel
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said any algorithm using only inner products can be lifted to a higher dimension, but nobody knows how to pick the best kernel. This extension asks whether the common hyperbolic-tangent kernel is always legal. The example was designed here: K equal to tanh of 2 times x transpose z plus 1 on the three points (-1, 0), (1.6, 0.9) and (0.1, -0.8) gives a Gram matrix with eigenvalues minus 0.132, 0.875 and 2.232. The result: a negative eigenvalue violates the Mercer condition; with 10 random points drawn 200 times the tanh kernel has a negative eigenvalue in all 200 draws and the Gaussian kernel in none. The meaning is that this choice of beta equal to 2 and gamma equal to 1 is not a legal kernel and the dual problem need not be convex, a theoretical inference and not measured here; check before using it, or use the Gaussian kernel. The next page poses an exercise.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the hyperbolic-tangent kernel can be illegal. This page poses an exercise back with the legal quadratic kernel: K equal to x transpose z plus 1, squared, with x equal to (1, 2) and z equal to (3, 1); the map has 6 features: 1, root 2 times x1, root 2 times x2, x1 squared, root 2 times x1 x2, and x2 squared. Question 1: compute K directly with the kernel. Question 2: compute the 6 features first, take their inner product and check it against Question 1. Work it out first, then see the next page.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed the exercise and this page is the complete solution. Question 1: x transpose z is 1 times 3 plus 2 times 1, which is 5, and K is 5 plus 1, squared, which is 36, with only 2 multiplications. Question 2: phi of x is (1, 1.414, 2.828, 1, 2.828, 4) and phi of z is (1, 4.243, 1.414, 9, 4.243, 1); the inner product is 1 plus 6 plus 4 plus 9 plus 12 plus 4, which is 36, the same as Question 1. Check: the same 36, the kernel works in 2-D while the map first builds 6 features, and the gap widens with dimension. That finishes the nonlinear SVM; the next knowledge point looks at the generalization of the kernel trick beyond the SVM and the kernel perceptron.

metadata.title: Pattern Recognition, Chapter 4, KP19: the nonlinear SVM and the Mercer kernel trick, a linear classifier in a space never visited (undergraduate, self-study)
